ja: ちゅうぎすいこぜんでん

p.src: The Grand Historian said, “The Difficulties of Persuasion and Solitary Indignation were written because sages and worthies gave voice to their indignation.” Seen in this light, the sages and worthies of old wrote nothing unless stirred by indignation. To write without indignation is like shivering when one is not cold or groaning when one is not ill—what could be more shameful? Even if such a work were written, what would there be to admire in it?

p.src: The Water Margin was written to give voice to indignation. For when the Song dynasty ceased to be strong, cap and shoes were worn upside down: the greatly worthy were placed below and the unworthy above, until even the northern tribes stood above while the Central Plain lay beneath them. Yet the sovereign and his ministers of that age remained like swallows and sparrows nesting in a hall, offering tribute, professing vassalage, and willingly bending the knee before those they scorned as dogs and sheep! Masters Shi and Luo lived under the Yuan, but their hearts remained with the Song; though born in Yuan times, they were in truth indignant over the affairs of the Song. Thus, indignant that the two emperors had been carried captive north, they told of the great defeat of Liao to vent their anger; indignant at the makeshift security sought after the court fled south, they told of the suppression of the three rebels to vent their anger. May I ask who it was that gave vent to this indignation? It was those very outlaws who once gathered in force by the marshes; one cannot but call them loyal and righteous. Therefore Masters Shi and Luo related the tale of the Water Margin and further named their tale Loyal and Righteous. Why loyalty and righteousness came to belong to the Water Margin may readily be understood; but why was every last member of the Water Margin band loyal and righteous? What drove them to it may likewise be understood.

p.src: It is a principle of things that those of lesser virtue should serve those of greater virtue, and the less worthy should serve the more worthy. But if a lesser worthy commands others while a greater worthy is commanded by them, would the latter willingly submit to such service without shame? It is like letting a weak man bind others while causing a strong man to be bound by them: would the strong man meekly offer his hands to be tied without protest? Such circumstances must inevitably drive all the mighty and worthy men under heaven into the Water Margin. Thus one may rightly say that the Water Margin band were all men of great strength and worth, possessed of loyalty and righteousness. Yet none possessed loyalty and righteousness to equal Song Gongming’s. The so-called hundred and eight shared merit and guilt, life and death alike; their loyal and righteous hearts resembled Song Gongming’s. Song Gongming alone, though dwelling amid the Water Margin, kept his heart fixed upon the imperial court. He sought amnesty with single-minded purpose and thought only of repaying the realm. In the end he faced great perils, accomplished great deeds, took poison and hanged himself, and did not shrink from dying with his fellows. Such was the fierce intensity of his loyalty and righteousness that it truly sufficed to win the hearts of all hundred and eight; hence he could bind them in brotherhood at Mount Liang and become their leader. In the final southern campaign against Fang La, more than half of the hundred and eight had already fallen in battle. Moreover, Zhishen passed away seated in meditation at Liuhe, Yan Qing tearfully took leave of his master, and the two lads followed a stratagem at Hunjiang. Song Gongming was not unaware of such things, but he held that perceiving the first signs of danger and wisely withdrawing was no more than a petty man’s scheme for preserving himself, something no man loyal to his sovereign and righteous toward his friends could deign to endure. This is what it means to be Song Gongming, and this is why the tale is called Loyal and Righteous.

p.src: Could such a tale have gone unwritten? Could such a tale go unread? Therefore, rulers of states cannot afford not to read it. Once they read this tale, loyalty and righteousness will no longer be found in the Water Margin, but wholly at the sovereign’s side. Worthy chief ministers cannot afford not to read it. Once they read this tale, loyalty and righteousness will no longer be found in the Water Margin, but wholly at the imperial court. The Ministry of War controls the vital machinery of military affairs, while regional commands bear sole responsibility for campaigns beyond the capital; they too cannot afford not to read it. If only they read this tale, then loyalty and righteousness will no longer be found in the Water Margin, but its men will all be chosen as the realm’s bulwarks and trusted confidants. Otherwise, if loyalty and righteousness are found neither at court, nor beside the sovereign, nor among the realm’s bulwarks and trusted confidants, where can they be? In the Water Margin. This is the indignation to which the tale gives voice. As for those fond of curious tales, they may draw conversational material from it, while men of war may borrow its stratagems; each merely discovers what suits his own strengths. But where in that do they perceive its vaunted loyalty and righteousness?
